content:
Plankton are the diverse collection of organisms found in water or air. They are unable to propel themselves against a current or wind. The individual organisms constituting plankton are called plankters. In the ocean, they provide a crucial food source to many small and large aquatic organisms. Bivalves, fish, and whales eat plankton. Marine plankton include bacteria, archaea, algae, protozoa, and drifting or floating animals. They live in the salt water of oceans and the brackish waters of estuaries. Freshwater plankton are similar to marine plankton but are found in lakes and rivers. Although plankton are mostly thought of as living in water, there are airborne versions as well. They live part of their lives drifting in the atmosphere. These aeroplankton include plant spores, pollen, and wind-scattered seeds. They may also include microorganisms swept into the air from dust storms or marine plankton swept into the air by sea spray.

Phytoplankton (plants) are some of the smallest life forms on Earth; scientists utilize microscopes to see them. Even though they are tiny, phytoplankton are vital to sustaining life on Earth. They are autotrophs, meaning they make their own food from photosynthesis. Like trees, they obtain energy from the sun; as a result, they live in the surface layers of oceans and lakes. Phytoplankton form the base of all marine and freshwater food webs. They are also key players in the global carbon cycle. They produce at least half of the oxygen on Earth but are only 1% of global biomass. Compared to terrestrial plants, phytoplankton are distributed over a larger surface area. Unlike trees that live for decades, they live and die in days. Phytoplankton are easily killed by changes in water temperature. As phytoplankton are at the bottom of the food chain and produce oxygen, it is important to consider how climate change affects them.

Ocean heat content is the energy absorbed and stored by oceans. It is clear that the ocean is warming due to climate change, and the rate of warming is increasing.  In 2022, the global ocean was the warmest it had ever been in recorded history. The upper ocean (above 2300 ft) is warming the fastest. However, the warming trend is global. The steady rise in ocean temperatures is unavoidable due to the Earth's energy imbalance. The root cause of the energy imbalance and the rising global temperatures is steadily increasing greenhouse gas emissions. These gases include carbon dioxide and methane. This leads to ocean warming because the ocean is sucking up most of the extra heat in the climate system. When the sea is warmer, water circulates less, making it harder for the sea to absorb more heat, and nutrient circulation decreases as well.

Ocean acidification is the decrease in the pH of the Earth’s oceans. In chemistry, pH is a scale used to specify the acidity or basicity of a liquid. Measurements of pH are important in chemistry, agronomy, medicine, water treatment, and many other fields. Between 1751 and 2021, the average pH of the ocean surface fell from about 8.25 to 8.14. That’s a nearly 30% increase in hydrogen ion concentrations in the world’s oceans. Carbon dioxide emissions from human activities are the main cause. Oceans absorb the CO2 in the atmosphere, which changes the pH of the ocean. Decreased ocean pH has a range of harmful effects on marine life. As a result, marine ecosystems are at risk, which puts food chains and oxygen-producing phytoplankton at risk. Ocean acidification has occurred previously in Earth's history. The resulting ecological collapse in the oceans had long-lasting effects on the global carbon cycle and climate.
